extracted.intended_audience: Authors, reviewers, meta-reviewers, and conference organizers of AI/ML conferences (ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS/etc.)
extracted.subtask_description: Position paper proposing concrete reforms to improve review quality in major AI conferences by adding author feedback, LLM-aware procedures, and systematic reviewer rewards. It targets changes to the double-blind conference peer-review workflow, reviewer incentives, and system-level tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage bi-directional review system (author feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-stage double-blind peer review system where authors evaluate reviews through objective criteria, with safeguards protecting reviewers from potential retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential process: release an initial, neutral/positive portion of reviews to authors (section one), collect author evaluations of those reviews, then release the critical portion (section two). Author feedback is used both short-term (context for meta-reviewers for that paper) and long-term (aggregated reviewer scores for rewards and accountability). Authors may flag suspected LLM-generated reviews during the feedback phase. Aggregated author feedback across multiple submissions provides a reliable measure while minimizing impact of retaliatory scoring; consistently low averages or repeated flags can trigger restrictions on reviewer appointments or manuscript submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage release of review content (content partitioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide review content into two distinct sections: section one includes neutral to positive elements (paper summary, strengths, clarifying questions) and section two contains critical parts such as weaknesses and overall ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential disclosure prevents retaliatory scoring and provides minimal safeguards for fair review. Authors complete their feedback on section one before seeing section two and cannot modify their evaluations afterwards. Practical notes: maintain existing timelines; ensure section one is informative enough to judge comprehension and constructiveness; use length limits on stage-one content to avoid gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author evaluation criteria: comprehension and constructiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors evaluate reviews from section one based on two key criteria: (1) the reviewer’s comprehension of the paper and (2) the constructiveness of questions in demonstrating careful reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objective criteria should be used in the feedback interface. Aggregation across multiple papers provides a more reliable signal of reviewer quality. To reduce retaliatory impact, authors’ evaluations are collected before the full review (ratings/weaknesses) are revealed. Systems should require justification when flags (such as LLM flags) are raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-generated review inclusion as deterrent and reference (LLM reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate LLM-generated peer reviews alongside human reviews during the second stage; the LLM review is exclusively visible to authors and they are explicitly informed of its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposes: (1) psychological deterrent against reviewers relying solely on LLMs, (2) provide a soft reference point for authors to identify and flag potential LLM-generated human reviews. Keep LLM service type and prompts confidential to reviewers; authors are not required to engage with LLM reviews. Meta-reviewers monitor aggregated LLM flags; repeated flagging may prompt actions. Systems must balance transparency and confidentiality of LLM provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM flagging and meta-reviewer oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may flag potential LLM-generated reviews when comparing human reviews to the provided LLM review; meta-reviewers review these flags and aggregated LLM flags inform decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require authors to provide specific justification when raising LLM flags to reduce misuse. Meta-reviewers should have visibility into per-paper flags and aggregated flags across reviewers; repeated LLM flags against a reviewer can trigger investigations or restrictions. Use flags as supplementary quantitative context, not sole evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length limitation on first-stage review content
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a length limitation on section-one (neutral/positive) review content to prevent reviewers from gaming author feedback by writing overly lengthy strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: elongated review bias (longer reviews rated higher even if informationally equivalent) can be exploited. Limit length to encourage concise but substantive summaries and clarifying questions. Pair length limits with quality-focused evaluation criteria (comprehension/constructiveness) to discourage verbosity-for-points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregated author feedback usage for meta-review decisions and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Author feedback scores on reviews are available to meta-reviewers as additional context for final decisions and are aggregated across a reviewer’s assignments to assess review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term: per-paper author feedback helps meta-reviewers assess the quality of reviews on that paper. Long-term: aggregated scores across submissions serve as quantitative metrics for reviewer quality. Consistently low aggregate scores or repeated LLM flags can lead to sanctions (e.g., restriction on future reviewer appointments, limits on submissions, or desk rejections) as already practiced in some venues (CVPR 2025 example). Use aggregated signals conservatively, with human oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer digital badge system (top 10% and 30%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement digital badges as visible credentials for reviewers (recommended top 10% and 30% reviewer badges) issued by conferences and displayable on academic profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Badges should follow standardized design/implementation policies across venues to remain meaningful. Use aggregated author feedback scores (and/or other tracking metrics) to determine eligibility. Limit badge diversity (e.g., top 10% and 30%) to avoid overload. Badges can serve as objective criteria when selecting leadership roles (area chairs, senior program members) and help make reviewer contributions professionally valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer activity tracking and reviewer impact score
rubrics_metrics.description: Track reviewer activity (document reviewer contributions to conferences) and create a reviewer impact score that quantifies the impact of the papers a reviewer reviewed (analogous to author h-index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage existing platforms (e.g., OpenReview, Publons) to document activity; respect anonymity options where appropriate. Reviewer impact score treats reviewers like authors, measuring contributions based on subsequent impact of reviewed works. This provides quantifiable portfolios reflecting both research and service; implementation requires System cooperation and careful design to avoid perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other reviewer rewards (in-kind compensation, symbolic recognition, workshops)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cost-effective tangible or symbolic rewards: in-kind compensation (registration fee waivers, subscriptions), specially marked conference name tags/merchandise, dedicated stickers, educational workshops, and citable proceedings documenting reviewing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey evidence suggests in-kind compensation effectively motivates reviewers; budget constraints require modest, visible rewards. Organize workshops where reviewers share practices and produce citable outputs, enhancing reviewer professionalization. Use a mix of symbolic and material rewards to raise visibility of review service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards and exemptions to protect reviewers from unfair evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: System-design options to protect reviewers include exempting reviewers from author feedback for desk-rejected or obviously low-value submissions and requiring justification for flags to prevent misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When papers are clearly filtered out (e.g., desk rejections), exempt associated reviewers from author feedback to avoid unfair evaluations. Require authors to provide specific reasons when flagging reviews (e.g., for suspected LLM generation) and rely on meta-reviewer oversight to adjudicate. Design exemptions to balance protection with accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Badge and reward eligibility design to prevent gaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Design evaluation metrics for badges and rewards that prioritize quality (thoroughness, identification of crucial issues, constructive feedback) over leniency, mere positivity, or length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reward rules that incentivize positive-only reviews. Use metrics that measure substantive contributions: technical depth, correctness, identification of critical issues, actionable suggestions. Combine author feedback with meta-reviewer signals to reduce manipulation. Monitor for gaming behaviors and iterate metric design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review quality dimensions and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Core dimensions for what constitutes a high-quality review: comprehension of the paper, technical depth, thoroughness, identification of crucial issues, and constructive feedback. Anti-patterns include superficial reviews, over-reliance on LLMs for technical judgment, and uninformative one-line comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation and reward systems should explicitly operationalize these dimensions (e.g., via author feedback prompts, meta-reviewer rubrics). Be aware of LLM shortcomings (current LLM-generated reviews often lack technical depth) and of biases such as author-outcome bias and elongated review bias. Combine multiple signals (author feedback, meta-reviewer judgment, length-normalized quality metrics) to assess quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual implementation: surveys and pilot programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Before broad adoption, conduct large-scale surveys of authors and reviewers to capture perspectives, and implement proposed changes as pilot programs in smaller tracks or workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys to understand distinct stakeholder responsibilities and challenges; pilot implementations help test feasibility and minimize disruption. Collect empirical evidence (e.g., effect on recruitment, review quality, gaming) and iterate before scaling to main conference tracks.
